description: We are a team passionate about technology, innovation, and space. We aim to learn, collaborate, and create meaningful solutions through the NASA International Space Apps Challenge. We welcome members with different skills and backgrounds who are eager to contribute, communicate, and grow together. Skills in programming, data, AI, design, GIS, or storytelling are welcome. Let’s build something impactful together!
summary: We developed AstroNova, an interactive web observatory designed to make NASA’s SPHEREx near-infrared all-sky survey and the search for hypothetical Planet X accessible to students, educators, and citizen scientists. The platform unifies five interactive modules: an orbital mission launchpad ("Beyond our Universe"), an All-Sky Infrared Atlas and Planet X Orbital Epoch Simulator (2025–2035) alongside a Cosmic Phenomena Tracker, a live observation Gallery connected directly to the NASA Image and Video Library API, a 102-channel spectrophotometric Data Lab featuring redshift simulation and CSV export, and an interactive spacecraft hardware schematic. By transforming complex infrared spectroscopy, biogenic ice absorption, and trans-Neptunian orbital dynamics into intuitive visual tools, our solution bridges open space data and public understanding. It empowers broader communities to explore how full-sky infrared surveys unlock cosmic history and outer solar system discoveries.
details:
AstroNova is an interactive astronomical visualization and education web platform centered on NASA’s SPHEREx near-infrared sky survey and outer solar system exploration (Planet X). It provides five integrated views: 

  1. Home ("Beyond our Universe"): Introduces the observatory concept, paired with four quick-access navigation cards to launch directly into celestial targets, galaxy imagery, cosmic phenomena, or spectral datasets. 
  2. Explore: Features three interactive workspaces:
  • All-Sky Infrared Atlas: Mollweide sky map with 6 LVF band filters (0.75–5.00 μm), toggleable sky layers, live RA/DEC tracking, and an object telemetry panel. 
  • Planet X Orbital Search: Outer solar system simulator (30–600 AU) comparing Trans-Neptunian orbits (e.g., 90377 Sedna) and Planet X across an epoch slider (2025–2035). 
  • Cosmic Phenomena Tracker: Summarizes four core SPHEREx science themes (Inflation, Biogenic Ices, Planet X Drift, and Reionization) linked to their spectra.
  1. Gallery: Showcases curated NASA observations alongside a live search bar connected to the NASA Image and Video Library API, complete with category filters, a high-detail lightbox modal, and an interactive false-color infrared simulation toggle. 
  2. Data Lab: Offers an interactive 102-channel near-infrared spectrophotometer (0.75–5.00 μm) with a live Redshift (z) slider, hover channel probe, downloadable CSV export, a 6-band spectral resolving power radar chart, and a sortable LVF focal plane calibration matrix. 
  3. About: Details the SPHEREx mission goals and provides an interactive spacecraft anatomy schematic (TPS-V3, OTA-200, FPA-102, BUS-BAES, EPS-SA2) plus four core science chapters. 

AstroNova runs as a responsive React and TypeScript web application that renders interactive sky maps, orbital trajectories, and 102-channel spectral charts directly in the browser using SVG. When users search in the Gallery, the app fetches live imagery and metadata from the official NASA Image (https://images.nasa.gov), while the Data Lab dynamically shifts simulated near-infrared spectral curves via the Redshift (z) slider and exports datasets as CSV files. 

By lowering the barrier to understanding infrared astrophysics, solid-state biogenic ice detection, cosmological redshift, and trans-Neptunian orbital clustering, AstroNova allows students, educators, and space enthusiasts to explore mission science visually without needing specialized scientific software. We aim to make NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey and outer solar system research engaging and intuitive for the public, while serving as an extensible frontend blueprint ready to ingest live public spectral releases in future iterations. 

Tools and technologies used include TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS, HTML5/CSS3, SVG, Phosphor Icons, the NASA Image (https://images.nasa.gov), Visual Studio Code, and GitHub. Large Language Models (LLMs) and AI coding assistants were also used to accelerate frontend prototyping, draft educational copy, and approximate the simulated 102-channel spectral curves.
